audience: This course is for beginners who want a practical, employable craft skill. Typical learners are one or more of Aspiring freelance video editors who want small paid jobs for local businesses
Church and mosque media volunteers who must turn service recordings into highlights and captioned sermons
Small-business owners and staff — restaurants, salons, shops, event centres, gyms — who have phone footage but cannot shape it into a promo
Content creators and social media managers who can shoot but want edits that look and sound professional
Event photographers and videographers who shoot but outsource (or avoid) editing
NYSC members and school leavers looking for a digital skill they can charge for in naira
Communication and media students needing practical post-production skill
Absolute beginners with basic phone or computer confidence
entry_requirements: There is no formal academic entry requirement. To join and benefit fully, a learner needs

Basic computer or smartphone confidence — opening an application, creating and saving a file, using a browser, copying files. This is assumed, not taught. A learner who cannot yet do this should take the CEA Computer Basics short course first
Access to a computer. Academy computers are provided; learners may bring their own laptop, but it is not required
A free CapCut account (email sign-up is enough), installed in Session 2
A USB flash drive of at least 16 GB for footage, project files and exports. Academy practice drives are available; learners who cannot bring one should tell the instructor at enrolment
Willingness to give and receive honest feedback on each other's cuts and to present work aloud in Session 9
Commitment to the ethics and copyright rules in Section 15
problem: Video Editing is a practical, beginner-level short course that turns a learner who can shoot or receive footage into someone who can organise, cut, sound-design, colour, caption, export and deliver a finished video. It is built around editing real clips in free software from the first session. Learners do not watch slides about editing — they edit.
